items.title: The Houses That Made New Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing
items.summary:
The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list r ecognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country— landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.

But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.

New Orleans, LA is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation .

“New Orleans itself is irreplaceable—not just one building, one district or one monument, but the entire living city,” said Kristin Gisleson Palme r, executive director of the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans when the title was announced.

Yet the buildings that earned the city that recognition now face a mounting threat: the cost of protecting them .

New Orleans has the second-highest homeowners insurance costs relative to property values among the nation's 100 largest metro areas, according to research from Realtor.com® . Now, as storms intensify and insurance costs rise , the city's historic homes are becoming more expensive to protect and preserve.

A city shaped by water 

On a recent walking tour through Bayou St. John , Heather Veneziano — director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program , who helped spearhead the city's nomination—began not with a building, but with the ground beneath our feet.

The bayou that gives the neighborhood its name connects to Lake Pontchartrain, a brackish estuary fed by rivers and linked to the Gulf of Mexico. The slower-moving waters served Indigenous communities as a transportation…
items.t: The Houses That Made New Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing

items.title: Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.28% Rate
items.summary:
Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up. 

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. 

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator , we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

Monthly mortgage payment today with a 20% down payment 

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000. 

At today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314. 

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more every single month.

Monthly mortgage payment today with a 3.5% down payment 

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and…
items.t: Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.28% Rate

items.title: Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs
items.summary:
A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

The Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at big energy infrastructure but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

The latest version released this month tweaked language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but still divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power .

"Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote, adding the bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run. 

But a range of housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. That includes the…
items.t: Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs

items.title: Boomers Disproportionately Own Homes in Top School Districts—but Aren’t Blocking Young Families, Study Claims
items.summary:
The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry . 

The Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

This is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there. 

Of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper says. 

Low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive , and homes there move faster,…
items.t: Boomers Disproportionately Own Homes in Top School Districts—but Aren’t Blocking Young Families, Study Claims

items.title: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion Valuation Exceeds the Worth of Every Home in San Francisco
items.summary:
Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the company’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

The Claude developer , which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The company sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate —and the statistics are shocking.

San Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

The aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's new valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

(Realtor.com) 

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are New York City, at $3.26 trillion,…

items.title: The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs
items.summary:
Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment . 

Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true. 

Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.

These programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable.

First-time homebuyers , often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help. 

The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan .

What are down payment assistance programs? 

Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment.

While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance , or PMI, which…
items.t: The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs

items.title: Thanksgiving Costs at Home Jump 6% in 2026 as Grocery and Utility Bills Hit Hosts Hard
items.summary:
Thanksgiving is the perfect time for loved ones to gather over a delicious, hearty meal. But in 2026, that feast could come with a higher price tag than we’d like.

According to the American Farm Bureau, the average cost of a 10-person holiday dinner will rise by 6% from 2025 to $5.86 per person . That’s because staples like turkey, milk, rolls, and cranberries have shot up in price.

And unfortunately, the higher price tag doesn’t stop at the grocery store. You may also notice a spike in your utility bills as your home’s systems are forced to work harder to keep everyone comfortable. 

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) found that the average family already uses over 300 gallons of water per day at home . With increased usage from additional showers, dishwashing, and hand-washing that are typical during the holidays, costs are sure to climb.

“Having guests over greatly drives up money spent on groceries, but it also drives up utility costs. Preparing all of that food often involves keeping ovens and burners running for multiple hours and using large amounts of water in both the cooking and cleaning processes,” explains Carrie Barnard , founder and recipe developer at Eating on a Dime .

Fortunately, it’s still possible to enjoy Thanksgiving without breaking the bank. A bit of planning and creativity can help keep your grocery expenses and utility bill in check.

items.t: Thanksgiving Costs at Home Jump 6% in 2026 as Grocery and Utility Bills Hit Hosts Hard

Ensani says the buyer, a man in the hospitality industry and his family, was—like all of the buyers in the boutique building—downsizing from a local "megaestate."

"The big thing that caught the buyer was a staff of 22 with armed guards," says the luxury broker. Additionally, the buyer, like many other high-net-worth individuals, was migrating to Beverly Hills in part because it has no so-called "mansion tax." 

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

items.title: What Every Home Needs for an Extended Power Outage

Americans are “pantry-loading” following a cascade of technology outages that have disrupted email, grounded flights, and interrupted banking services—while feuling fears that the failures could be signs of something bigger .

Costco and Walmart have reported increased purchases of emergency supplies, from food and water to batteries and generators. As of Nov. 15, 21 of the 26 high-priced generators offered on Costco's website were sold out, according to Bloomberg .

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales," David Bellinger , an analyst for Mizuho , a Japanese investment bank, wrote in a recent research note.

Federal officials say they've found no evidence that the outages are connected or resulted from coordinated cyberattacks. But while the fears driving the rush to stockpile may be unfounded, the threat of prolonged disruptions is all-too real.

In August, severe storms knocked out power to nearly 375,000 customers across Northwest Indiana , leaving some without electricity for nearly two weeks.

A historic ice storm in January caused more than 330,000 outages across Mississippi and Louisiana , where some residents faced similarly long waits.

Both emergencies stretched far beyond the familiar three-day supply of food and water—and exposed how quickly households can lose access to basic necessities.

“A three-day emergency kit is still a good starting point, but I’d consider it the minimum…
items.t: What Every Home Needs for an Extended Power Outage

items.title: Mortgage Rates Surge Again as Stubborn Inflation Ends Brief Reprieve
items.summary:
Mortgage rates are rising again after four consecutive weeks of declines, as hotter-than-anticipated inflation data sets the stage for another interest rate hike, putting upward pressure on Treasury yields. 

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac . For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

"While prospective borrowers often shop around for a home, they may not always think to do the same for their mortgage, as comparing multiple rate quotes can potentially save them thousands over a loan's lifetime," says Sam Khater , Freddie Mac's chief economist.

The October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report came in above expectations last week on both the headline and core measures, all but guaranteeing that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Dec. 8. 

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 5% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again. 

"The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith . "That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market."

Markets are currently pricing a 93% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales…
items.t: Mortgage Rates Surge Again as Stubborn Inflation Ends Brief Reprieve

items.title: Damaged Building Next to Brooklyn Collapse Scene Will Be Demolished
items.summary:
A Brooklyn apartment building adjacent to the site of last week's deadly building collapse is set to be demolished after city officials determined that it was unsafe to enter.

On Nov. 11, the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. suddenly collapsed, killing eight people, including two children, and injuring 18 others.

When 1321 Flatbush collapsed, it took the adjoining wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. with it, leaving the apartments in that building exposed to the elements. Striking images from the scene showed the perfectly undisturbed apartment interiors of 1323 Flatbush just as tenants had left them as they rushed to escape. 

The collapse occurred while workers were doing excavation work at 2625 Bedford Ave., adjacent to 1321 Flatbush—a job site that had a history of safety violations, including proceeding with demolition in defiance of a stop-work order, according to the Department of Buildings.

The city has opened an investigation into the cause of the collapse and is doing sweeps of more than 160 work sites across the city associated with the construction team at 2625 Bedford Ave.

”If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a press conference last week.

Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez has also opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse. No charges have been filed yet.

Displaced tenants of both buildings are staying in hotels provided by the American Red Cross through the end of November and the Department of…
items.t: Damaged Building Next to Brooklyn Collapse Scene Will Be Demolished

A CT scan also showed a tumor on his left kidney. After a series of tests and appointments, he learned it was cancer—a revelation he had kept private for months.

"This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life. Back in July, I woke up one morning in horrible pain and ended up in the hospital with kidney stones. What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined," he penned on his candid social media post. 

Jax Taylor had been quietly facing one of the most frightening chapters of his life while settling into a new home with his son, Cruz. (Instagram)

It’s crazy how you can act like everything is normal when deep down you’re a mess."

items.title: Family Found Dead in Foreclosed Home Survived Months Longer Than Previously Thought
items.summary:
New evidence suggests that at least one member of a family found dead inside a foreclosed-upon Connecticut home survived longer than previously thought—paving the way for transfer of title to a new owner. 

The bizarre case hinges upon whether the home's owners died before or after the foreclosure was recorded. If the owners were already dead at the time of the filing, the foreclosure may be deemed illegitimate, and a search for rightful heirs would begin.

Edward Marchion stumbled into the mystery in June, when he purchased 7 Stanwich Lane , a four-bedroom, three-bathroom home in Burlington, CT , in a foreclosure auction for $525,000. The 2,800-square-foot home sits on more than 2 acres and comes with a hot tub, patio, and deck, according to the listing.

A few days after placing the winning bid, Marchion finally entered the property and came across a grisly sight. The skeletal remains of the property’s previous owners, Sally Anne Cash and Paul Cash , and their adult son Brian Cash , were found inside. 

Marchion then asked a judge to halt the closing on the property to determine the timeline of the Cashs’ deaths. 

In a July 2 filing in the state Supreme Court, Marchion’s lawyer John C. Lewis III asked the court to delay closing until the Connecticut State Police could determine whether the Cash family died before or after the foreclosure action.

"From a title perspective, unless it can be determined that the Defendants were alive on the date the lis pendens was recorded (August 6, 2025), then the foreclosure action is defective," wrote Lewis.

Now, months later, new…
items.t: Family Found Dead in Foreclosed Home Survived Months Longer Than Previously Thought

items.title: Anthropic’s Blockbuster IPO Set To Spark a New San Francisco Housing Frenzy: ‘Expect More All-Cash Offers’ and Bidding Wars
items.summary:
Real estate agents in San Francisco are bracing for further acceleration of the housing market as Anthropic makes an initial public offering at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion.

The Bay Area has been a hot spot for newly wealthy AI trendsetters in recent years, rebuilding a market that was left hurting during the COVID-19 pandemic as tech offices emptied. With major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic planting roots in San Francisco, the housing market has grown competitive, leading what some real estate agents are calling a “ mansion shortage .”

Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO went live on Thursday, marking one of the largest public-market debuts in history.

The Claude developer, which will trade under the ticker ANT, initially said it planned to price shares at between $70 and $78, which would value the company at between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Late Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported the company planned to debut at $83 per share, taking the valuation to $1.5 trillion.

In addition to the public offering, Anthropic is set to receive an extra $26 billion in a private placement sale of shares to several other major tech companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and more, according to Yahoo Finance .

While employees and insiders won't see cash in hand until after a significant lockup period, the debut could give many early shareholders the confidence to move forward with real estate purchases.

“Confidence may change before purchasing power does. There are lockup periods, taxes, and individual circumstances to consider, so I…
items.t: Anthropic’s Blockbuster IPO Set To Spark a New San Francisco Housing Frenzy: ‘Expect More All-Cash Offers’ and Bidding Wars

items.summary:
We would like to hear from private tenants about their experiences of the rental deposit system in England

In May 2026, the government overhauled private renting by abolishing no-fault evictions and shifting private tenancies to rolling contracts. However, deposit protection remains an issue for many private renters.

The government has promised and begun consulting on reforms, including scrapping insured deposit schemes, but has yet to confirm when this will happen. Landlords and letting agents are currently permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts and this creates a “power imbalance”, housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook has said.

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.
